title: Which creases of your paper protractor cut an angle in half?
description: An angle bisector is a crease that cuts an angle into two equal angles, and the creases OE and OC of the paper protractor are bisectors, checked by folding. Keeko's doubt, that a bisector can cut an angle into parts of any size, is broken by folding along an unequal crease.
teaching_notes: One idea: a bisector cuts an angle into two equal angles that fit on each other. Watch for children who call any crease inside an angle a bisector.

source: Identify the angle bisectors in your handmade protractor. Tr
video_script.why: The child finds angle bisectors among the creases of the paper protractor and checks them by folding.
video_script.substitution: A folded paper corner, whose crease makes two angles that fit on each other.
video_script.anchor: the book's unfolded paper protractor with the creases OA to OI along the straight edge
video_script.wrong_answer: a bisector can cut an angle into two parts of any size
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a bisector can cut an angle into two parts of any size. A crease that leaves one part bigger will not fold onto the other part, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Crease O E and crease O C are angle bisectors

final_answer.value: OE bisects ∠AOI (90° each side); OC bisects ∠AOE (45° each)
final_answer.spoken: crease O E bisects the straight angle into two angles of ninety degrees, and crease O C bisects the right angle into two angles of forty five degrees

maths_rules: an angle bisector cuts an angle into two equal angles
OE bisects the straight angle AOI: 180 / 2 = 90 degrees each side
OC bisects the angle AOE: 90 / 2 = 45 degrees each
check by folding: along OE, OA lands on OI; along OC, OA lands on OE
OB cuts AOE into 22.5 and 67.5, which are unequal, so OB is not a bisector of AOE
video_script.design: The unfolded protractor stays on the board. The statement that OE bisects the straight angle is written only in the answer beat; the steps show the angles on each side.

<bookmark mark='split'/>The crease O E splits it into two angles. Each is ninety degrees.

<bookmark mark='again'/>Fold along O C, and O eigh lands exactly on O E.

beats.on_screen: Answer: OE bisects ∠AOI (90° each side); OC bisects ∠AOE (45° each)

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Crease O E and crease O C are angle bisectors.
<bookmark mark='why'/>O E cuts the straight angle into two angles of ninety degrees. O C cuts the right angle into two angles of forty five degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko says a bisector can cut an angle into two parts of any size.
<bookmark mark='try'/>Try the crease O B in the right angle between O eigh and O E. It makes twenty two point five and sixty seven point five.
<bookmark mark='fold'/>Fold along O B, and O eigh does not land on O E. A bisector must cut the angle into two equal parts.
